source.title_on_document: AI-assisted design synthesis and human creativity in engineering education

supplement.where: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frai.2026.1714523/full#supplementary-material (p. 9, Supplementary material). Appendix A (photographs of the workshop) and Appendix B (both surveys) are referred to on p. 4 and p. 5 and are not in this PDF.
supplement.holds: Appendix A: photographs of the workshop set-up. Appendix B: the pre- and post-surveys. The main text does not say that the supplement holds any further statistics.

paper_design_summary: In a 90-minute workshop, volunteers (postgraduate students, early-career lecturers, industry mentors) self-organized into teams of two to three, and each team drew an envelope that assigned it to ChatGPT-4 access with a standard prompt sheet or to no LLM (non-LLM web resources allowed). Teams had 45 minutes to design and build a tabletop catapult. Outcomes were team-level answers to post-survey questions on number of designs considered, variety of mechanical principles, uniqueness of the final design, and how well the catapult worked, compared with Mann-Whitney U tests over 7 AI and 5 non-AI teams.

studies.label: Catapult Challenge workshop (AI-assisted vs non-AI teams)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition (ChatGPT-4 access with prompt sheet vs no LLM) was assigned to self-organized teams by each team's representative drawing one of 12 shuffled opaque envelopes (7 'AI group', 5 'non-AI group'). Team membership itself was self-selected before assignment.
assignment.quote: the session chair prepared 12 shuffled, opaque envelopes (seven designated as "AI group" and five designated as "non-AI group"), and immediately before the task, one representative from each self-organized team drew an envelope to determine random condition assignment.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; also p. 7, Section 4 ("The condition assignment was randomized at the team level")

arms.name: AI-assisted teams
arms.description: Uninterrupted browser access to ChatGPT-4 (web version 2025-03-13) plus a standardized prompt sheet asking for three catapult concepts; teams free to refine, modify, or disregard the suggestions.

arms.name: Non-AI (control) teams
arms.description: Could sketch freely and consult non-LLM web resources such as Wikipedia or YouTube; told explicitly that large language models were prohibited.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions reported. Missing values were less than 2 percent across all items (p. 5, Section 2.3). The paper never states the number of individual participants. Team counts: AI = 7 teams, non-AI = 5 teams (p. 5, Section 3), i.e. 12 teams analyzed, matching the 12 envelopes; but p. 4 says participants 'self-organized into eight teams of two to three members each', which conflicts with 12. With 2 to 3 members per team, 12 teams would hold at most 36 people (my arithmetic, not stated in the paper).
participants.who: Convenience cohort of volunteers: postgraduate students, early-career lecturers, and industry mentors; 85 percent engineering background, 62 percent male, 30 percent under 34 and 70 percent aged 45 or older.
participants.country: Not stated explicitly; authors at Nazarbayev University, Astana, Kazakhstan, and the ethics statement cites the data protection laws of the Republic of Kazakhstan (p. 8).
participants.quote: A convenience cohort of volunteers, comprising postgraduate students, early-career lecturers, and industry mentors, self-organized into eight teams of two to three members each.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; team counts p. 5, Section 3 ("The sample size is AI = 7 teams; non-AI = 5 teams.")

ai_tool.how_used: Browser access throughout the 45-minute task, with a standardized prompt sheet: 'Suggest three distinct catapult concepts using only craft sticks, rubber bands, and a spoon...'. Teams could refine, modify, or disregard the suggestions (p. 4, Section 2.1).

task.description: Catapult Challenge (adapted from Seelig 2017): design and build a functional tabletop catapult from craft sticks, rubber bands, plastic spoons, masking tape, a marble, and scissors that launches a marble at least 50 cm, with access to a testing station.

outcomes.name: Quantity: number of catapult designs the team considered
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Post-survey item 'How many catapult designs did your team consider?' on a 5-point scale (1 design to 5+ designs), answered by participants right after the task. Two raters only transferred the categorical responses to a coding sheet (kappa = 0.94). How individual answers became one team value is not stated.

contrasts.reported: Non-AI 60% (3 out of 5) considered three or more design variants vs 0% of AI-assisted teams; U = 6, p = 0.073, effect size r = -0.52. Figure 1: AI teams 14.3% 1 design, 85.7% 2 designs; non-AI teams 40.0% 2 designs, 40.0% 3 designs, 20.0% 4 designs.

outcomes.name: Variety: whether designs used different mechanical principles
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Post-survey item 'Did designs employ different mechanical principles?' on a 3-point scale (0 = no variety, 1 = medium variety, 2 = distinct variety).

contrasts.reported: Text: "40% vs. 29% achieving distinct principles with U = 11.5, p = 0.373, and r = -0.26". Figure 2 (left): non-AI 40.0% no variety, 20.0% medium, 40.0% distinct; AI 57.1% no variety, 42.9% medium, 0% distinct. The text's 29% for AI conflicts with the figure.

outcomes.name: Uniqueness of the final design
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Post-survey item 'How unique was your final design?' on a 3-point scale (0 = standard design, 1 = somewhat unique design, 2 = unique design).

contrasts.reported: Non-AI 40% rated final designs "very unique" vs 14% (1 out of 7) of AI teams; U = 8.5, p = 0.168, r = -0.40. Figure 2 (right): non-AI 20.0% standard, 40.0% somewhat unique, 40.0% unique; AI 71.4% standard, 14.3% somewhat unique, 14.3% unique.

outcomes.name: Quality: how well the catapult worked
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Post-survey item 'How well did your catapult work?' on a 3-point scale (0 = failed, 1 = worked somewhat, 2 = worked well). Teams had a testing station, but the recorded outcome is the survey answer, not a measured launch distance.

contrasts.reported: All non-AI teams (100%) "worked well" vs 29% (2 out of 7) of AI-assisted teams; U = 5.0, p = 0.051, r = -0.56. Figure 3: AI 71.4% worked somewhat, 28.6% worked well; non-AI 100.0% worked well.

company_involvement.description: Funded by Nazarbayev University (Grant Agreement No. 201223FD8810, FDCRG); authors declare no commercial relationships.
company_involvement.locator: p. 8, Funding; p. 9, Conflict of interest

eligibility.reason: Condition was randomly assigned to self-organized teams by envelope draw (p. 4), so criterion 1 is met at the team level, although the authors call the design quasi-experimental. The paper never gives a count of people; it analyzes 12 teams (7 AI, 5 non-AI, p. 5) of two to three members (p. 4), at most 36 people, so criterion 2 fails. All four creativity outcomes are participants' own post-survey answers about their team's designs (p. 4-5), not ratings by raters or computed measures, so criterion 3 fails. Belongs in the screening report as a small randomized experiment with self-reported outcomes.

one_line_finding: Across 7 ChatGPT-4 teams and 5 non-AI teams building a catapult, non-AI teams reported more designs considered (U = 6, p = 0.073), more variety (p = 0.373), more unique final designs (p = 0.168), and better-working catapults (100% vs 29% worked well, U = 5.0, p = 0.051), none significant at 0.05 (p. 5, Section 3.1).
open_questions: Number of teams: p. 4 says participants self-organized into eight teams, but 12 envelopes were prepared and the analysis uses AI = 7 and non-AI = 5 teams (p. 5).
The number of individual participants is never stated.
Variety: the text gives 29% of AI teams achieving distinct principles, but Figure 2 shows 0% distinct variety for AI teams (57.1% none, 42.9% medium).
All participants filled the post-survey with team-level items; the paper does not say how individual answers were combined into one value per team.

Section 3.1 says Uniqueness was 'approaching significance', but its p-value (0.168) is the second largest; Quality (p = 0.051) is the closest to 0.05. Section 3.2 says non-AI teams 'significantly outperformed' AI teams, which conflicts with the non-significant tests.
notes: The control arm could consult non-LLM web resources (Wikipedia, YouTube), so I coded the contrast ai_vs_active; whether control teams used them is not reported. Individual-level outcomes (pre-post creative self-efficacy, divergent-thinking confidence, problem-solving efficacy, innovative-thinking self-ratings; Wilcoxon |z| < 1.2, p > 0.20, p. 5, Section 3.2) are self-perceptions of ability, not scored on output, and are not listed as outcomes. Statistics are Mann-Whitney U, p, and effect size r per outcome plus percentage distributions in Figures 1 to 3; no means or SDs are printed. Data availability: raw data 'will be made available by the authors without undue reservation' (p. 8). The candidate record's design guess 'other' and question guess 'with_ai' are consistent with this reading except that assignment was randomized at team level.
